\subsection{Sharp Detection Onset}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, Granger-causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (3~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression across the 13-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ at $T{=}10$, steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$, $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the sharp detection onset is specification-invariant.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, 24/24 forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance with 0/24 reverse (4~seeds); directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).\footnote{Seed~43 at $\alpha{=}0.10$ shows 3/8 PermG FDR-significant pairs versus 0/8 for seed~42, consistent with stochastic variation at low signal rather than robust detection; no other below-threshold $\alpha$ level exhibits seed-dependent detection.}
Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable Granger-causal signal in the canary metrics.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{Metric trajectories at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds). Token entropy drops at generation~1; distinct-1 declines from generations~2--3, with a consistent one-generation canary lead across all four seeds (shaded: inter-seed range). This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant pairs.}
\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8 both seeds; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 0--6/8 per seed, 2 of 3 seeds ${\geq}5/8$; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
At $\alpha{=}0.55$, PermG returns 0/8 FDR-significant pairs despite marginal $p$-values ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}}{=}0.062$--$0.092$), consistent with power-limited non-detection between onset and synchronous dip; differenced cross-correlation detects 8/8 bidirectionally at this level, confirming that a lead-lag signal exists but falls below PermG's directional detection threshold.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, forward-direction significance rates range from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 37.5\% (PermG), with inter-method $\kappa = 0.185$ (near chance) and a spurious rate of at least 62.5\%.
PermG achieves the lowest null-control FPR among directionally-specific methods (11.1\%, 4/36 across 6 seeds; DiffXCorr achieves 2.8\% but lacks directional separation) with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}); its nonparametric null distribution, built-in directionality, and hyperparameter-free design explain this advantage.
The $S \times R$ framework generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$ via $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ should left-shift, (ii)~the transition should smooth, and (iii)~different methods should exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values.
These predictions are under empirical verification.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_dose_response.pdf}
\caption{PermG forward detection rate across 13 contamination levels (Pythia-410M, fp32, direction-checked). Four regimes: blind ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8), onset ($\alpha{=}0.50$, 6/8), synchronous dip ($\alpha{=}0.60$, 0/8), and detection ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 0--6/8).}
\label{fig:regime_map}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Forward-direction FDR significance rates (\%) across contamination levels (Pythia-410M, seed~42, fp32, direction-checked). Each cell: fraction of 8 validated pairs at BH-corrected significance ($q{=}0.05$). PermG achieves the lowest null-control FPR (11.1\% pooled across 6 seeds) with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$.}
\label{tab:method_comparison}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Method & $\alpha{=}0.0$ & $\alpha{=}0.25$ & $\alpha{=}0.50$ & $\alpha{=}0.75$ & $\alpha{=}1.0$ & FPR$_\text{null}$ \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\subsection{Cross-Architecture Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate the sharp detection onset across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B parameters, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} reports PermG forward detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}$6/8 in 11 of 15 conditions (73\%).
Non-confirming conditions span precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16: 0/8 vs fp32: 6/8), bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43: 6/8 both directions), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B: s42 2/8, s43 6/8), and entropy decoupling (SmolLM3-3B: 3/8, entropy 0/4).

\label{sec:intervention}

We implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ switches to $0.0$ (pure real data).
A reactive baseline triggers when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$.
The predictive trigger fires at generation~1 in both Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32), one generation before the reactive baseline (generation~2).
Peak perplexity under predictive intervention is $56.99$ versus $157.09$ under reactive (s42 fp32), a 58\% reduction (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%).
Recovery occurs at generation~2 under predictive cessation versus generation~4 under reactive.
Both models converge to the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline by generation~10.

The trigger generation, recovery timeline, and convergence behavior are identical across the $3.4\times$ scale gap from 410M to 1.4B, and the 15\% entropy threshold generalizes without recalibration.
These results position canary-based detection within a four-layer taxonomy of collapse monitoring: (1)~dimensionality collapse, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.10$ via $n$-gram diversity decline; (2)~distributional variance, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.25$ via calibration drift; (3)~causal coupling, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ via Granger precedence; and (4)~dynamical stability, assessable at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ via lag structure.
Each layer captures a distinct aspect of collapse, and lower layers activate at lower contamination thresholds.
The practical implication is that canary monitoring should combine multiple detection layers rather than rely on any single statistical test.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""T=20 post-analysis: run D120 5-method lead-lag + verify against locked predictions."""

import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys

PROJECT_ROOT = "/root/autodl-tmp/distrib_canary_collapse"
ANALYSIS_SCRIPT = os.path.join(PROJECT_ROOT, "run_5method_analysis_d102.py")
N_PAIRS = 8


def check_experiment_complete(exp_dir, expected_gens=21):
    """Check that all gen_0..gen_{expected_gens-1} have metrics.json."""
    missing = []
    for g in range(expected_gens):
        mpath = os.path.join(exp_dir, f"gen_{g}", "metrics.json")
        if not os.path.exists(mpath):
            missing.append(g)
    return missing


def run_5method(exp_dir, alpha, seed):
    """Run the D120 5-method analysis script and return the JSON result path."""
    cmd = [
        sys.executable, ANALYSIS_SCRIPT,
        "--data_dir", exp_dir,
        "--alpha", str(alpha),
        "--seed", str(seed),
    ]
    print(f"Running: {' '.join(cmd)}")
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(result.stdout)
    if result.returncode != 0:
        print(f"STDERR: {result.stderr}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    json_path = os.path.join(exp_dir, "analysis", "5method_leadlag.json")
    if not os.path.exists(json_path):
        print(f"ERROR: expected output not found: {json_path}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    return json_path


def load_predictions(pred_path, alpha):
    """Load the locked prediction for a given alpha."""
    with open(pred_path) as f:
        data = json.load(f)

795	\section{PermG FPR Independence Analysis}
796	\label{app:fpr_independence}
797	
798	Table~\ref{tab:null_fpr_methods} reports null-control FPR for all five detection methods across six seeds ($6 \times 6 = 36$ pairs, 6-pair basis excluding mauve).
799	Under identical BH-FDR correction ($q{=}0.05$), DiffXCorr achieves the lowest FPR (1/36, 2.8\%) but lacks directional separation; PermG (4/36, 11.1\%) is the lowest among directional methods.
800	All four PermG false positives occur in token\_entropy$\to$distinct pairs (seeds~45 and 50, forward direction only), suggesting a structural pattern concentrated in a single canary--downstream pair type.
801	
802	\begin{table}[h]
803	\centering
804	\small
805	\caption{Null-control FPR by method ($\alpha{=}0.0$, 6~seeds 45--50, 6~pairs each). All p-value--based methods (DiffXCorr, PermG, TY) report BH-FDR--corrected rejections at $q{=}0.05$ for fair comparison. Threshold uses a deterministic $3\sigma$ criterion; NaiveXCorr uses uncorrected correlation significance.}
806	\label{tab:null_fpr_methods}
807	\begin{tabular}{llrr}
808	\toprule
809	Method & Criterion & Rejections (/36) & FPR (\%) \\
810	\midrule
811	Diff.\ XCorr$^\dagger$ & BH-FDR & 1 & 2.8 \\
812	\textbf{Perm.\ Granger} & \textbf{BH-FDR} & \textbf{4} & \textbf{11.1} \\
813	Threshold & $3\sigma$ (det.) & 10 & 27.8 \\
814	Toda--Yamamoto & BH-FDR & 14 & 38.9 \\
815	Naive XCorr & uncorr. & 33 & 91.7 \\
816	\bottomrule
817	\multicolumn{4}{l}{\footnotesize $^\dagger$Bidirectional; cannot separate forward from reverse.} \\
818	\end{tabular}
819	\end{table}
820	
821	\paragraph{Cluster adjustment.}
822	The 36 null-control pairs are nested within 6~seeds (6~pairs per seed), introducing within-seed correlation.
823	Within-seed ICC${=}0.14$ yields an effective sample size $N_{\text{eff}} \approx 21$ (from $N_{\text{eff}} = N / [1 + (m-1) \cdot \text{ICC}]$ where $N{=}36$, $m{=}6$).
824	Under the Clopper--Pearson exact method with $N_{\text{eff}}{=}21$ and 4 successes (scaled), the cluster-adjusted 95\% CI is $[1.2\%, 30.4\%]$, compared to $[3.1\%, 26.1\%]$ under independence ($N{=}36$).
825	The lower ICC compared to the 3-seed pilot ($0.14$ vs.\ $0.34$) reflects greater between-seed consistency with six independent replications.
826	
827	\paragraph{Direction filtering.}
828	Forward-direction filtering (retaining only pairs with peak lag${<}0$ for cross-correlation methods) reduces null-control $K{\geq}3$ false positives.
829	Under the 6-seed, 6-pair basis, $K{\geq}3$ consensus with filtering produces 6/36 false positives (16.7\%; detail below); the 3-seed pilot underestimated this rate (0/8).
830	Detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ is unaffected: $K{\geq}3$ counts are identical with and without direction filtering at all signal levels.
831	
832	\paragraph{$K{\geq}3$ false positive detail.}
833	Under the 6-pair basis (6~seeds, 36~pairs), $K{\geq}3$ consensus produces 6 false positives (FPR${=}16.7\%$).
834	Of these, 4 are driven by naive cross-correlation, threshold onset, and Toda--Yamamoto (PermG does \emph{not} vote); the remaining 2 (seeds~45 and 50, te$\to$distinct) include PermG in the consensus.
835	PermG thus contributes to only 2 of 6 consensus false positives, confirming that most $K{\geq}3$ FPR is driven by the high-FPR methods (naive, threshold, TY).
836	
837	\paragraph{Sensitivity to FPR assumption.}
838	Even under the conservative upper bound of the cluster-adjusted CI (30.4\%), PermG remains the lowest-FPR directional method: DiffXCorr achieves a lower FPR under identical BH-FDR correction (2.8\%) but lacks forward/reverse separation; the next directional method (threshold onset) has 27.8\% and Toda--Yamamoto 38.9\%.
839	Our primary results rely on equal-weight $K{\geq}3$ majority voting, where each method contributes exactly one vote regardless of its FPR---this mechanism is completely unaffected by any FPR assumption.
840	For the exploratory FPR-inverse weighting, PermG's weight ($w{=}1/0.111{=}9.0$) exceeds all directional alternatives (threshold: 3.6, TY: 2.6, naive: 1.1); DiffXCorr ($w{=}1/0.028{=}35.7$) receives a higher weight but lacks directional separation, preserving PermG's rank among directional methods.
841	The insensitivity of both the voting mechanism and the method ranking to the upper CI bound provides evidence that the MMCT conclusions are robust to uncertainty in PermG's Type~I error rate.
842	
843	\section{Sigmoid Transition Shape}
844	\label{app:sigmoid_shape}
845	
846	Sigmoid regression on the original 13-point $T{=}10$ grid yields $\alpha_c = 0.483 \pm 0.006$ but $k = 478 \pm 475$ ($\mathrm{SE}(k) \approx k$), indicating that the coarse grid cannot constrain the transition shape.
847	Dense $\alpha$ sampling (17~values at $T{=}10$) resolves this ambiguity: formal likelihood-ratio testing strongly favors a smooth sigmoid over a literal step function ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC}{=}-110$), with fitted steepness $k{=}15.7$ (95\% CI $[9.4, 28.2]$).
848	The transition is steep but finite-width, not a literal discontinuity.
849	This observed steepness exceeds what smooth signal models predict: VAR(1) simulations under H0 (linear, $k{=}6.1$) and H0$'$ (concave, $k{=}4.9$) produce onset sigmoids with $k{=}4.9$--$6.1$ (\S\ref{app:power_sim}), yielding steepness ratios $k_{\mathrm{obs}} / k_{\mathrm{H0}} \approx 2.6$--$3.2$ (CI lower bound ratio ${\approx}2$).
850	We do not fit a combined $T{=}10 + T{=}20$ sigmoid because $\alpha{=}0.45$ yields contradictory counts under the two sequence lengths (0/8 vs.\ 5/8), reflecting genuine power dependence on $T$ rather than a single dose-response curve.
851	
852	
853	\section{Intervention Threshold Sensitivity}
854	\label{app:intervention_sensitivity}
855	
856	\paragraph{Within-$\alpha$ sensitivity at $\alpha{=}1.0$.}
857	Table~\ref{tab:threshold_sensitivity} reports the predictive cessation outcome under five entropy-drop thresholds (5\%--25\%) at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, seed~42).
858	All five thresholds produce identical outcomes: token entropy drops 40.7\% at generation~1, far exceeding even the most conservative threshold (25\%), so every threshold triggers at the same generation.
859	The intervention conclusion---peak perplexity 57.0, recovery in one generation, final perplexity 21.3---is invariant to threshold choice within this range.

\section{Sigmoid Transition Shape}
\label{app:sigmoid_shape}

Sigmoid regression on the original 13-point $T{=}10$ grid yields $\alpha_c = 0.483 \pm 0.006$ but $k = 478 \pm 475$ ($\mathrm{SE}(k) \approx k$), indicating that the coarse grid cannot constrain the transition shape.
Dense $\alpha$ sampling (17~values at $T{=}10$) resolves this ambiguity: formal likelihood-ratio testing strongly favors a smooth sigmoid over a literal step function ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC}{=}-110$), with fitted steepness $k{=}15.7$ (95\% CI $[9.4, 28.2]$).
The transition is steep but finite-width, not a literal discontinuity.
This observed steepness exceeds what smooth signal models predict: VAR(1) simulations under H0 (linear, $k{=}6.1$) and H0$'$ (concave, $k{=}4.9$) produce onset sigmoids with $k{=}4.9$--$6.1$ (\S\ref{app:power_sim}), yielding steepness ratios $k_{\mathrm{obs}} / k_{\mathrm{H0}} \approx 2.6$--$3.2$ (CI lower bound ratio ${\approx}2$).
